content: Prompted voiding is a behavioral therapy primarily utilized in North American nursing homes. Its purpose is to enhance bladder control in individuals, regardless of whether they have dementia, by employing verbal prompts and positive reinforcement techniques. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of prompted voiding in managing urinary incontinence in adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register (as of January 31, 2006) and reference lists of relevant articles. Investigators in the field were also contacted to identify additional studies. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated the use of prompted voiding for managing urinary incontinence. Participants in these trials were adult men and women, with or without cognitive impairments, who were diagnosed with urinary incontinence based on symptom classification or urodynamic testing as determined by the trialists. The identified studies were assessed for eligibility, and two independent reviewers evaluated the methodological quality of the selected trials. Data related to six pre-specified outcomes were extracted independently by each reviewer, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. When additional clarification or details were needed, trial investigators were consulted. A third reviewer was involved to proofread the review at various stages. A total of nine trials were included in the review, involving 674 elderly participants, most of whom were women. These trials compared prompted voiding with no prompted voiding. The limited evidence suggested that prompted voiding led to an increase in self-initiated voiding and a reduction in episodes of incontinence in the short term. However, there was no evidence to determine whether these effects were sustained over a longer duration of prompted voiding or if they persisted after the intervention was discontinued. The authors concluded that the evidence was insufficient to make definitive recommendations for clinical practice. While there was some indication of short-term benefits from prompted voiding, the long-term effects remain unknown. Additionally, the implementation of prompted voiding requires significant resources, which must be considered.
